newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Last HK governor shuns good-luck rite at farewell.
newsitem.headline: Last HK governor shuns good-luck rite at farewell.

text.p: Britain's last colonial governor Chris Patten--the man Beijing says will be "cursed for a thousand generations"--ignored a good-luck custom on Monday when he finally left his Hong Kong mansion.
He received a grand send off from the stately home where he has lived and orchestrated democratic reforms for the past five years, angering the communist Chinese government.
Under a steady drizzle, police cadets with rifles and fixed bayonets ringed the circular driveway and honour guards from the still-Royal Hong Kong Police performed a silent drill.
To the astonishment of staff and onlookers, Patten broke with tradition and failed to perform an "I will return" ritual in which departing governors circle the front drive three times.
"I don't know what happened," said Paul Brown, a Patten spokesman who was as amazed as everyone else. Patten made only one circle in a Rolls Royce before sweeping through the imposing gates.
Patten's job ends at midnight on Monday when the British colony reverts to China, ending 156 years of British rule.
The "last colonial tyrant", as Patten often described himself in self-mockery, wore a dark blue suit and blue tie. He watched silently from a small podium.
His arrival in Hong Kong earlier dressed in a business suit instead of the white uniform, feathered pith helmet and sword of previous colonial governors had endeared him to the people of Hong Kong.
To the pipes and silver bands of the police band playing "My home" he bid farewell to his aides and front office staff. Many dabbed their eyes.
Household staff, in their white uniforms with red trimming, and their families watched silently. They had said their goodbyes earlier.

To the notes of the "Last Post", traditional military farewell played by a lone bugler, the Governor's Standard -- a British union flag with the Hong Kong crest in the centre -- was slowly lowered from the podium of Government house, carefully folded and presented to Patten as the drizzle grew stronger.
The crowds massed outside Government House and in the skyscrapers overlooking the mansion, cheered when he received the standard.

Patten, despite his verbal battles with China over limited democratic reforms for Hong Kong was a genuinely popular leader, revered for his common touch, in stark contrast to the aloof style of his predecessors.

To a speeded up rendition of "Auld Lang Syne", his motorcade swept out of Government House, Patten and wife Lavender in the leading Rolls Royce and his three daughters, Kate, Laura and Alice in the Daimler following behind.

After attending an outdoor British farewell ceremony and a banquet and solemn flag change ceremony marking the transfer of British rule to China at midnight, Patten will sail into history on the royal yacht Britannia.

The staff of Government House had little time to rest. When midnight strikes, they remove the British Queen Elizabeth's portrait, the royal coat of arms, and the colonial crests from the walls and gates of Government House.
Police will drop the royal prefix and don new badges and insignia, devoid of crowns and other symbols of British rule.

The mansion, which once dominated the city but is now dwarfed by skyscrapers, will become a post-colonial government guesthouse and venue for state functions because future leader Tung Chee-hwa has chosen against taking up residence.
He said Chinese geomancers have declared it inauspicious. Part of it may be turned into a museum.
